title: Russell, Karpinska, Iyyer: People who frequently use ChatGPT for writing tasks are accurate and robust detectors of AI-generated text (ACL 2025)
topic: what readers key on in 300 non-fiction articles
rule: Heavy LLM users catch AI articles (majority vote of 5 misses 1 of 300; mean 92.7% true-positive). Their stated clues, by share of explanations: vocabulary 53.1%, sentence structure 35.9%, grammar/punctuation 24.8% (AI too polished), originality 23.7% (safe, predictable, no surprise or humour), quotes 22.3%, clarity 19.5% (over-explains, irrelevant detail). Casual contractions and 'just'/'actually' read as human.
example: 'not only ... but also ...'; lists of exactly three; 'testament', 'crucial'; quotes sound formal and too like the surrounding prose, and sit at paragraph ends
llm_tell: Over-polished grammar; predictable safe content; not-only-but-also and triples; over-explaining with irrelevant detail; quotes in the narrator's own register placed at paragraph ends; stock vocabulary.

title: GPTZero on Graphite's AI-written web study
topic: prevalence and reach of AI articles
rule: Graphite sampled 55,400 English Common Crawl URLs with three detectors (Pangram, GPTZero, Copyleaks): AI-primary share was 36% within a year of ChatGPT and 48% by two years, then flat near 50%. AI articles largely do not appear in Google or ChatGPT citations (86% of Google top-ranked articles human; 82% of ChatGPT/Perplexity-cited human). It reports no stylistic traits, only detector output.

title: Paul Graham: Write Simply / Write Like You Talk
rule: Write in spoken language. Test each sentence: would I say this to a friend? If it clanks, replace it with what you would say; read drafts aloud; for a stiff draft, explain it to a friend and use that. Hard subjects get no more complex sentences than everyday talk.
example: 'the mercurial Spaniard himself declared' fails the friend test; 'pen' as a verb fails
llm_tell: Elevated, nominal, writerly phrasing nobody would say aloud ('the mercurial Spaniard' register) in a plain explanation.

title: Paul Graham: Writing, Briefly
topic: how a good essay is made
rule: Try to tell the reader something new and useful. Write a fast rough draft, then rewrite repeatedly and cut anything unnecessary; print it out; read aloud and mark paragraphs you dread reading as boring; tell real surprises from digressions and park digressions in footnotes. Conversational tone, short Germanic words, no trying to sound impressive. Write for a skimmer. If stuck, say the most important sentence first, or say it to someone and write down what you said.
llm_tell: An LLM draft is usually first-draft-final: no cuts, no digression discipline, nothing new, so the skimmer finds nothing to keep.

title: APS Observer: The Curse of Knowledge (Pinker)
rule: Chief cause of opaque writing is forgetting what the reader doesn't know. Define jargon, spell out intermediate steps that feel too obvious, describe the concrete scene or procedure instead of the abstract finding, show early drafts to a representative reader (empathy alone doesn't fix it; people guess others' minds badly), rewrite several times for clarity alone, cut 'soggy apologies and hedges' (somewhat, nearly, apparently). Classic style: the writer shows the reader something they can see, in plain declarative steps.
example: Rabbit-illusion rewrite: taps moving up the arm, instead of the abstract result
llm_tell: The inverse failure: an LLM has no curse of knowledge and over-defines everything, including what the reader knows, while still skipping the real unobvious step. Fix: name the reader, then define only what that reader lacks.

title: Julia Evans: a year explaining computer things
rule: Explain what you just learned, starting from the basic question ('what does a shell even do?'). Learn and teach by trying things and breaking them; give readers the tool to do the same. Lead with a tl;dr; headings as plain questions; casual first person; say what you don't know; be specific and quantified. Keep a topic narrow (via podcast snippet): specificity respects the reader's time and gives more context than a survey.
example: Headings like 'what does "explain computer things" mean?'; counts like 11 zines, about 370,000 words
llm_tell: LLM explainers survey the topic from nowhere with no first-person trial, no thing the author broke, and no admitted uncertainty.

title: Julia Evans: how I made a zine (snippet via search)
rule: Zines are first-person and about one really specific thing. Comics are not the point: making something a cartoon does not by itself teach what people need.

title: Worked-example effect / expertise reversal (search snippets: Kalyuga, Ayres, Chandler, Sweller 2003; Van Gog, Kester, Paas 2011; Wesenberg 2022)
rule: Novices learn more from studying a worked solution before attempting problems than from solving cold; the advantage vanishes or reverses as expertise grows (expertise reversal), so unneeded steps become redundant load. Fix: fade steps out gradually or use completion tasks. Correct example before an erroneous one gave lower mental load. Primary papers not read; secondary summaries only.
llm_tell: LLM tutorials give every step at one density for an unnamed reader. Fix: state who the reader is, fully work the first case, then leave later steps for them.

title: Blog on McPhee's Draft No. 4, 'Structure' chapter (snippet, secondhand)
rule: McPhee sorted overwhelming notes into piles only after writing a lead sentence, and settled the ending before going back to write the opening. He arranged pieces on index cards until the order was fixed, and wants structure not to be noticed. Not read in his own words (New Yorker excerpt blocked to the fetch tool).
example: Encounters with the Archdruid, 34 cards in rows, order unchanged through months of writing
llm_tell: LLM structure is announced (headings, signposts, 'In this article we will') and the ending summarises instead of being the place the piece was heading.

title: Zinsser on writing well (search snippets; book not read)
rule: Strip every sentence to its cleanest components: cut adverbs that repeat the verb, passives that hide the actor, long words for short. Writers sell their identity, candor and point of view. Lead and ending advice not obtained in any source.

title: Search roundup of blog/forum AI tells (Decoder, Ministry of Testing, Grammarly)
rule: Weak evidence: forum users cite formulaic 'In conclusion' wrap-ups that restate, paragraphs that each expand one brief thought, uniform sentence length. The one measured piece is a word-frequency study of 2024 science abstracts, where 'delves', 'showcasing' and 'underscores' ran up to 25 times above trend. No controlled human-vs-AI tutorial comparison was found.
example: 'In today's fast-paced world', 'delve into', 'at its core'
llm_tell: Generic scene-setting opener; restating conclusion; each paragraph a single expanded thought with even length.

title: Not obtained within budget
rule: No evidence read for: Zinsser on leads and endings, Wait But Why, Stripe docs as a documented exemplar, Pinker's classic-style chapter in his own words, McPhee in his own words, or any controlled test of tutorial-order for written how-tos. New Yorker blocked to the fetch tool.
